extracted.intended_audience: Recipients of federal funds (LEAs, IHEs), State athletic associations, school administrators, Title IX coordinators, policymakers, and public commenters
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating or drafting sex-related eligibility criteria for student participation on male or female athletic teams consistent with gender identity, to ensure compliance with the Department's proposed §106.41(b)(2) standard and related regulatory requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed §106.41(b)(2) standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the proposed regulation, a recipient would be permitted to adopt or apply sex-related eligibility criteria that would limit or deny a student's eligibility to participate on a male or female athletic team consistent with their gender identity only if those criteria, for each sport, level of competition, and grade or education level, (i) are substantially related to the achievement of an important educational objective, and (ii) minimize harms to students whose opportunity to participate on a male or female team consistent with their gender identity would be limited or denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central two-part test the Department proposes recipients must satisfy before imposing sex-related eligibility criteria. It must be applied on a sport-by-sport, competition-level, and grade/education-level basis. The RIA frames this as both a legal standard (substantial relation to an important educational objective) and a harms-minimization requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize potential harms in designing criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must design sex-related criteria to minimize potential harms imposed on affected students (e.g., difficulty of obtaining documentation, risk of invasion of privacy or disclosure of confidential information).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department gives concrete examples of harms to consider (documentation burdens; privacy/confidentiality risks). If a recipient can reasonably adopt or apply alternative criteria that cause less harm and still achieve its important educational objective, the recipient must adopt the less-harmful alternative and may not adopt the more-harmful criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: No broader-than-necessary sex-based classifications (narrow tailoring)
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient is precluded from implementing sex-based classifications more broadly than is necessary to implement the statute's underlying goals, consistent with Title IX's nondiscrimination guarantee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department emphasizes that any sex-based distinction must be limited to what is necessary to achieve the asserted educational objective and must be consistent with Title IX's prohibition on sex discrimination. Overbroad classifications that extend beyond what is necessary are impermissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sport-, level-, and grade-specific permissibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The permissibility of particular sex-related eligibility criteria may differ depending on the sport, level of competition, grade or education level, or other considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department asks whether and how permissibility should vary by sport, competition level, or grade. It notes examples (NCAA and national governing bodies using sport-by-sport approaches; some international/elite-level rules differ markedly) to illustrate that different sports and competition tiers may justify different criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special consideration for earlier grades
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether any sex-related eligibility criteria can meet the proposed standard when applied to students in earlier grades, and if so, the types of criteria that may meet the proposed standard for those grades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department specifically invites comment on whether criteria appropriate at higher levels of competition would meet the standard for elementary or middle school students, recognizing that many State athletic policies are silent regarding elementary students and vary for middle school.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to select less burdensome regulatory approaches (RIA/EO 13563 principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: In choosing among alternative regulatory approaches, the agency must tailor regulations to impose the least burden consistent with obtaining regulatory objectives; select approaches that maximize net benefits; specify performance objectives rather than prescribing means of compliance where practicable; and identify and assess available alternatives to direct regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The RIA cites Executive Order 13563: (1) benefits must justify costs; (2) tailor to impose least burden; (3) choose approaches that maximize net benefits (including distributive impacts and equity); (4) specify performance objectives if feasible; (5) identify alternatives (economic incentives, information). Recipients and commenters should consider these principles when proposing or evaluating regulatory alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for clear regulatory text and guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether regulatory text in addition to the proposed paragraph is needed to provide recipients with sufficient clarity on how to comply with Title IX's prohibition on sex discrimination, including gender identity discrimination, in the context of male and female athletic teams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department asks if further clarifying language or additional regulatory provisions should be included to help recipients understand and implement the standard (e.g., examples, procedural rules, or definitions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize harms to students whose eligibility is limited or denied
rubrics_metrics.description: How a recipient can minimize harms to students whose eligibility to participate on a male or female athletic team consistent with their gender identity is limited or denied by the recipient's adoption or application of sex-related criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department solicits comment on concrete practices recipients could adopt to reduce harms (procedural safeguards, privacy protections, reduced documentation burdens, alternative participation opportunities), emphasizing that minimizing harms is an explicit component of the proposed standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility decision-making process transparency and allocation of authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies should make clear who determines eligibility (school, school plus student, athletic association, or other body), because current State variation leaves eligibility decisions at differing levels of authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department observed variation—nearly half of States leave decisions to the school or school and student-athlete; ~30% involve the athletic association. Recipients should clarify decision procedures, appeal processes, and roles to ensure consistent, fair application of criteria and compliance with Title IX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation criteria and burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of documentation-based eligibility requirements used by some State athletic associations include written statements from the student, parent/guardian, health care or treatment provider, or community member/teacher identifying the student's consistent gender identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department notes both the types of documentation used and the potential burden/difficulty of obtaining such documentation. When designing documentation requirements, recipients should weigh privacy, accessibility, and the potential for unequal burdens on students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for State laws, State athletic association policies, and litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must account for the wide variation in State laws and State athletic association policies (ranging from full inclusion to categorical exclusion) and ongoing litigation that may affect the applicability or enforceability of State restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department observed that ~20 States have laws explicitly requiring participation consistent with sex assigned at birth, while others require participation consistent with gender identity or impose varying criteria. Recipients should monitor state law, association rules, and court decisions when developing policies and consider how indirect effects (e.g., association rules) may affect entities not directly subject to the regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sport- and competition-level medical or physiological criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Some governing bodies apply medical/physiological criteria (e.g., testosterone suppression, puberty history) for eligibility—often varying by sport and level of competition—and recipients should consider whether such criteria satisfy the substantial-relation and harms-minimization standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department cites examples (NCAA sport-by-sport deferral to national governing bodies; some international bodies permit transgender women if testosterone suppression criteria are met; others exclude transgender women who experienced male puberty). Recipients should evaluate whether such sport- or level-specific medical criteria are substantially related to important educational objectives and whether they can be applied without undue harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use best-available evidence and quantify costs/benefits where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory decisions and recipients' policy choices should rely on best available techniques to quantify anticipated present and future benefits and costs as accurately as possible, and the Department solicits data on affected populations, participation rates, and time estimates for compliance activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The RIA describes limitations (inability to quantify many benefits), presents the Department's best estimate of net costs ($23.4M–$24.4M over 10 years), and invites commenters to provide data sources and disaggregated estimates. Recipients and commenters should support policy choices with empirical data where feasible and comment on the reasonableness of modeling assumptions.
